transcript.en: Our class kept a reading diary for a term. Students who read more often scored higher in the reading test. Could we predict a new student's mark from their reading hours? Today: how a straight line can predict, and when not to trust it. A model is a simple rule learned from data that makes a prediction. The simplest model is a straight line through a scatter plot. Finding that line is called linear regression. Many lines could pass through the dots. The best fit line keeps the gaps between the dots and the line as small as possible. The computer finds it in a moment. Here are average marks for pupils grouped by hours of reading each week. They climb steadily, about two marks for every extra hour. The line has a slope and a start. Here the slope is two marks per hour, and the start is eight marks for no reading. So the prediction is eight plus two times the hours. Careful with lines. Our pupils read between zero and five hours, so the line only knows that range. And a line shows a pattern, not a promise for one pupil. Quick check! The slope is two marks per hour. If a pupil reads three more hours a week, how many more marks does the line predict? Six more marks. Three hours times two marks per hour is six. That is what slope means: the change for each extra unit. In the app, open the scatter lab and show the line of best fit. Drag one pupil far from the others and watch the line tilt. Your turn. Our pupils read up to five hours. Should we trust the line to predict the mark for forty hours a week? No, forty hours is far outside our data. Remember: the best fit line is a model, its slope is the change per unit, and it only works inside the data you had. Try it yourself: measure the height and arm span of a few people, and lay a ruler where the line fits best. Predict someone new, then measure and compare.

body.en:
A model is a rule learned from data that makes predictions. Linear regression fits the straight line y = a + bx that makes the squared vertical gaps between the points and the line as small as possible (least squares). The slope b = Σ(x − x̄)(y − ȳ) ÷ Σ(x − x̄)², and the line always passes through the point of means, so a = ȳ − b × x̄.

Read the slope as change per unit: if mark = 8 + 2 × hours, each extra hour of revision goes with 2 more marks on average. The intercept is the prediction at x = 0.

Two limits matter. Interpolation, predicting inside the range of your data, is reasonable; extrapolation far outside it is a guess with no evidence. And a fitted line describes an association, not a cause.
body.ar:
النموذج قاعدة متعلَّمة من البيانات تقدّم تنبؤات. ويوفّق الانحدار الخطي الخط المستقيم ص = أ + ب س الذي يجعل مربّعات المسافات الرأسية بين النقاط والخط أصغر ما يمكن (المربّعات الصغرى). والميل ب = مج(س − س̄)(ص − ص̄) ÷ مج(س − س̄)²، ويمرّ الخط دائمًا بنقطة المتوسطين، فيكون أ = ص̄ − ب × س̄.

steps.solution:
x = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
y = [10, 12, 14, 16, 18]
mx, my = 3, 14
sxy = sxx = 0
for i in range(5):
    sxy += (x[i] - mx) * (y[i] - my)
    sxx += (x[i] - mx) ** 2
b = sxy / sxx
a = my - b * mx
print(round(a + b * 6, 1))

transcript.en: Last year our school used a model to predict which students would pass. On last year's students it was right every time. This year it was wrong for one student in three. Today: why we test a model on data it has never seen. The fix is simple. Split your data before you start: about eighty percent to train the model, and twenty percent locked away to test it. The test set plays the part of next year's pupils. A model can remember its training pupils without learning anything useful. The test pupils are new to it, so its score on them is an honest guess of how it will do next year. Here is the test error as we make the model more and more complex. It falls at first, then rises again. The middle model is the best one for new pupils. A model that bends to fit every training pupil is overfitting. It learns the noise, like one pupil's lucky day, as if it were a rule. It looks perfect in training and fails on new data. One rule matters most. Never peek at the test set while you build the model. If you tune the model to the test pupils, the test stops being fair. Quick check! A model scores one hundred percent on its training pupils and sixty percent on the test pupils. Which score tells you how it will do next year? The test score, sixty percent. The perfect training score only shows the model remembered its pupils. The big gap is a sign of overfitting. In the app, open the overfitting lab. Raise the complexity slider and watch the training error fall while the test error turns back up. Your turn. Why do we keep twenty percent of the data away from the model while we build it? To check it on pupils it has never seen. Remember: train on most of the data, test once on the rest, and a big gap between the two scores means overfitting. Try it yourself: make a rule from ten cards, then test it on five hidden cards. Did your rule still work on the cards it had never seen?

body.en:
A model can score perfectly on the data it learned from and still fail on new data, because it can memorise examples instead of learning a general rule. So we split the data before building anything: typically 80% as the training set and 20% as the test set. We fit the model on the training set and evaluate it once on the test set, which estimates performance on unseen data.

Overfitting is when a model fits noise in the training data. The sign is a low training error with a much higher test error. Underfitting is the opposite: a model too simple to capture the pattern, with both errors high. The best model sits between the two.

The test set must stay untouched. If you keep adjusting the model to improve its test score, the test becomes part of training and your estimate becomes optimistic.
body.ar:
قد يحصل النموذج على درجة كاملة مع البيانات التي تعلّم منها ثم يفشل مع بيانات جديدة، لأنه قد يحفظ الأمثلة بدل أن يتعلّم قاعدة عامة. لذلك نقسّم البيانات قبل بناء أيّ شيء: عادةً ٨٠٪ مجموعة تدريب و٢٠٪ مجموعة اختبار. ونوفّق النموذج على بيانات التدريب ونقيّمه مرة واحدة على بيانات الاختبار، فيقدّر ذلك أداءه مع بيانات لم يرها.

الإفراط في التوفيق هو أن يوفّق النموذج الضوضاء في بيانات التدريب. وعلامته خطأ تدريب منخفض مع خطأ اختبار أعلى كثيرًا. والتفريط عكسه: نموذج أبسط من أن يلتقط النمط، وكلا الخطأين مرتفع. وأفضل نموذج يقع بينهما.

ويجب أن تبقى بيانات الاختبار دون لمس. فإذا ظللت تعدّل النموذج لتحسين درجة الاختبار، صار الاختبار جزءًا من التدريب وصار تقديرك متفائلًا.

transcript.en: A new student joined our class in March. Our teacher had her reading speed and her accuracy from a short test. Which reading group should she join? Today: how a model can sort new cases by looking at the closest old ones. Regression predicts a number, like a mark. Classification predicts a label, like a reading group or a type of fruit. The model learns from examples that already have labels. Put every pupil on a scatter plot, speed across and accuracy up, coloured by group. Put the new pupil on it too. The nearest neighbour method gives her the group of the closest pupils. Here are her five nearest classmates by group. Three are in the blue group, and one each in red and green. The vote says blue. Closest means the shortest distance on the chart. We find it with Pythagoras: the square root of the gap in speed squared plus the gap in accuracy squared. Make the two measures use similar scales first. The number of neighbours we ask is called k. With k equal to one, a single odd pupil can decide. A small odd number such as three or five is a good start. To choose between them, hold back some training pupils as a validation set: they pick k, and the test set stays locked away. Quick check! With k equal to three, two neighbours are in group A and one is in group B. Which group does the model choose? Group A, by two votes to one. The model simply copies the most common label among the nearest examples. That is why it is easy to explain to pupils. In the app, open the nearest neighbours lab. Drop a new point, change k, and watch the regions of each colour grow and shrink. Your turn. A model chooses a reading group for a new pupil. Does it predict a number or a label? A label, so it is classification. Remember: place the new case, find the k nearest examples by distance, and take the most common label. Try it yourself: weigh some fruit at home and score their colour from one to five. Then find the three nearest neighbours of a mystery fruit.

body.en:
Regression predicts a number; classification predicts a label, such as the type of a fruit. k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) is a simple classifier. Store every labelled example as a point described by its features, say weight and a colour score. To classify a new point, compute its distance to every example, take the k closest, and predict their most common label.

Distance is usually Euclidean: d = √((x₁ − x₂)² + (y₁ − y₂)²). Features must be on comparable scales; otherwise the one measured in larger units, like grams, dominates. A common fix is to rescale each feature to the range 0–1.

The choice of k matters. With k = 1 the model follows every odd example and overfits; a very large k blurs the classes together. Choose k with a validation set: a slice of the training data you hold back just for comparing values of k, so the final test set stays untouched. Use an odd k for two labels to avoid ties.
body.ar:
يتنبأ الانحدار برقم، ويتنبأ التصنيف بتسمية، كنوع الفاكهة. وأقرب k جيران مصنِّف بسيط. خزّن كل مثال له تسمية نقطةً تصفها خصائصها، كالوزن ودرجة اللون. ولتصنيف نقطة جديدة، احسب مسافتها إلى كل مثال، وخذ أقرب k، وتنبّأ بالتسمية الأكثر بينها.

والمسافة عادةً إقليدية: م = √((س١ − س٢)² + (ص١ − ص٢)²). ويجب أن تكون الخصائص بمقاييس متقاربة، وإلا سيطرت الخاصية المقيسة بوحدات أكبر، كالجرامات. ومن الحلول الشائعة إعادة قياس كل خاصية إلى المدى ٠–١.

واختيار k مهم. فمع ⁦k =⁩ ١ يتبع النموذج كل مثال غريب ويفرط في التوفيق، ومع k كبيرة جدًا تختلط التسميات. اختر k ببيانات التحقق: جزء من بيانات التدريب تحجزه لمقارنة قيم k فقط، فتبقى بيانات الاختبار النهائية دون لمس. واستعمل k فردية مع تسميتين لتجنّب التعادل.

transcript.en: Our school tried a model to warn us early about pupils who might need extra help. It was ninety percent accurate. Then we noticed it had not warned us about a single pupil. Today: how to judge a model by the mistakes it makes. Accuracy is the share of cases the model gets right. But if only one pupil in ten needs help, a model that always says no help is already ninety percent accurate. Accuracy alone can hide a useless model. A model can make two kinds of mistake. A false alarm warns about a pupil who is fine. A miss stays quiet about a pupil who really needs help, and at school a miss usually costs more. We count all four results for one hundred pupils. Eight were caught, two were missed, six were false alarms and eighty four were rightly left alone. Many models give each pupil a score from zero to one. We choose a threshold, and pupils above it get a warning. Lower the threshold and you catch more pupils, but you also raise more false alarms. Choosing the threshold is not a maths question. A false alarm costs a student a short chat, while a miss can cost a student a year. So the school chose a low threshold, and a person always checks each warning. Quick check! One pupil in ten needs help, and a model always says no help. It is ninety percent accurate. Is it a good model? No. It misses every single pupil who needs help. Always look at the misses and the false alarms, not only the accuracy. In the app, open the threshold lab. Slide the threshold down and up, and watch the four boxes of the confusion matrix change. Your turn. What happens when we lower the threshold for a warning? We catch more pupils, and we get more false alarms. Remember: accuracy can hide misses, count both kinds of mistake, and let people choose the threshold. Try it yourself: keep a rain forecast for a week, and note whether it rained each day. body.en:
Accuracy is the share of predictions that are correct, but it can mislead when classes are imbalanced. If 1 email in 10 is spam, a filter that never flags anything is 90% accurate and useless.

A confusion matrix counts four outcomes: true positives (TP, correctly flagged), false positives (FP, false alarms), false negatives (FN, misses) and true negatives (TN). From it come precision = TP ÷ (TP + FP), the share of flags that were right, and recall = TP ÷ (TP + FN), the share of real positives that were caught.

Many classifiers output a score, and a threshold turns it into yes or no. Lowering the threshold raises recall but usually lowers precision. The right threshold depends on the costs: missing a disease is worse than a false alarm, while a spam filter that hides real mail is worse than letting some spam through.

الدقة نسبة التنبؤات الصحيحة، لكنها قد تضلّل حين تكون إحدى التسميتين أندر كثيرًا من الأخرى. فإذا كانت رسالة واحدة من كل ١٠ مزعجة، فالمرشّح الذي لا يعلّم شيئًا أبدًا دقته ٩٠٪ وهو عديم الفائدة.

وتعدّ مصفوفة الالتباس أربع نتائج: الإيجابيات الصحيحة (مُعلَّمة بحق)، والإيجابيات الكاذبة (إنذارات كاذبة)، والسلبيات الكاذبة (فوات)، والسلبيات الصحيحة. ومنها تأتي الضبطية = الإيجابيات الصحيحة ÷ (الإيجابيات الصحيحة + الكاذبة)، أي نسبة الحالات المُعلَّمة التي كانت صحيحة، والاستدعاء = الإيجابيات الصحيحة ÷ (الإيجابيات الصحيحة + السلبيات الكاذبة)، أي نسبة الحالات الإيجابية الحقيقية التي التُقطت.

تُخرج مصنِّفات كثيرة درجة، وتحوّلها العتبة إلى نعم أو لا. وخفض العتبة يرفع الاستدعاء لكنه يخفض الضبطية عادةً. والعتبة المناسبة تعتمد على التكلفة: ففوات مرض أسوأ من إنذار كاذب، بينما مرشّح الرسائل الذي يُخفي بريدًا حقيقيًا أسوأ من تمرير بعض الرسائل المزعجة.
